title: HOTA: Hamiltonian framework for Optimal Transport Advection
claim: Our method transports source distributions to targets along smooth, obstacle-avoiding optimal trajectories across both smooth and non-smooth cost landscapes.
layout: 2x3 grid of scatter/trajectory plots; top row smooth potentials, bottom row non-smooth obstacles; source on left (red), target on right (green)
description: Six matplotlib-style 2-D panels in two rows of three. The top row shows smooth potentials: two elongated blue Gaussian bumps (Stunnel), a narrow hourglass-shaped blue region (Vneck), and a GMM with a ring of red source points sending trajectories outward to eight green clusters. The bottom row shows non-smooth hard-obstacle potentials in dark blue: BabyMaze with two staggered walls, Slit with a vertical wall and a central gap, and Box with a central square. In every panel, red source points sit on the left (or center for the GMM), black target points sit on the right, and green mapped points overlap the black targets. Many pastel dashed trajectory lines connect source to target and bend around the high-potential blue regions. Axes have numeric ticks and there are no titles or legends inside the panels.
caption: Evaluation of HOTA method on smooth (top) and non-smooth datasets (bottom): Stunnel, Vneck, GMM, BabyMaze, Slit, Box. Blue regions indicate high values of potential $U(x)$. Distributions $\alpha$ (red), $\beta$ (black) and the mapped $T_\#\alpha$ (green).
abstract: Optimal transport (OT) has become a natural framework for guiding the probability flows. Yet, the majority of recent generative models assume trivial geometry (e.g., Euclidean) and rely on strong density-estimation assumptions, yielding trajectories that do not respect the true principles of optimality in the underlying manifold. We present Hamiltonian Optimal Transport Advection (HOTA), a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman based method that tackles the dual dynamical OT problem explicitly through Kantorovich potentials, enabling efficient and scalable trajectory optimization. Our approach effectively evades the need for explicit density modeling, performing even when the cost functionals are non-smooth. Empirically, HOTA outperforms all baselines in standard benchmarks, as well as in custom datasets with non-differentiable costs, both in terms of feasibility and optimality.
